text: If you took the accounting fundamentals course, you've met the idea that revenue is recognized when it's earned, not necessarily when cash or an invoice shows up. Let's close chapter three by seeing how that shows up specifically inside Receivables transactions.

Every transaction line recognizes revenue one of two ways. Immediate, the full amount in the same period it's accounted, right for most straightforward product sales. Or deferred, spread across multiple periods using a revenue scheduling rule, because what's being billed is actually delivered over time, like a twelve-month subscription. This is purely an accounting decision, it doesn't change when the invoice is sent or when cash is collected.

A revenue scheduling rule controls how that spread works. Fixed schedule, a defined number of periods in equal or specified amounts. Daily revenue rate, based on actual days in each period, which handles partial first and last periods more precisely. Until revenue is recognized, the unrecognized part sits in unearned revenue, a liability, not a revenue account.

Picture Northwind Fixtures Co selling Harborline Retail Group a twelve-month maintenance contract for twelve thousand dollars, invoiced in full upfront. The line uses a deferred rule, twelve equal monthly periods. At completion, the invoice books a debit to Accounts Receivable and a credit to Unearned Revenue for the full amount. Then each month, one thousand dollars moves from Unearned Revenue to Revenue, even though Harborline already paid in full back in January. That closes chapter three. Chapter four moves to Transactions, starting with creating receivables invoices.
